stories.title: Florida Voters Approve Property Tax Cuts, Raising Questions for CRE
stories.excerpt: Florida voters approved far-reaching property tax cuts in Tuesday’s election, which proponents say will slash the budgets of local governments, although the impact on the real estate industry remains unclear. The measure, known as Amendment 3, won 62 percent of the vote, surpassing the 60 percent threshold required to alter the state’s constitution. The measure would halve the annual cap on increases to commercial properties and second homes, but the biggest tax cuts target primary residences. The homestead exemption, which reduces the taxable assessed value of a primary home, is set to triple to $150,000 next year, then increase to $250,000 the following year, with subsequent hikes tied to inflation. Florida does not have a state income tax, so most county and city governments rely heavily on property taxes. The changes are expected to cost local governments $4.6 billion in 2027, $8.4 billion the following year, and nearly $12 billion in 2032, according to analysis from the Florida Legislature. To blunt the cuts in property tax revenue, some counties and municipalities are expected to raise millage rates, the basis for calculating property taxes, and fees, including those for permits — potentially eroding the touted savings. As homeowners receive the largest tax breaks, local governments may also become increasingly reliant on commercial properties for revenue, and could decide to increase their taxes. Landlords, in turn, could raise rents to offset the higher costs, passing the burden to tenants. Take multifamily properties, whose tax bills could climb nearly 15 percent, or about $406 per unit, according to a study by Jared Walczak, a senior fellow at the Washington-based Tax Foundation and president of Walczak Policy Consulting. It’s unclear whether Amendment 3 will boost the housing market and entice new-to-market buyers. To qualify for the cuts, property owners must be Florida residents before the end of the year. Afterward, transplants must wait five years. Co
bullets: Florida Amendment 3 approved with 62% vote; halves cap on commercial property tax increases
Homestead exemption triples to $150K next year, reaches $250K following year, then inflation-indexed
Revenue loss projected at $4.6B (2027), $8.4B (2028), $12B (2032) for local governments
stories.summary: Florida voters approved Amendment 3, which cuts property taxes on primary residences by tripling the homestead exemption to $150,000 immediately and $250,000 the following year, with subsequent increases tied to inflation. The measure also halves the annual cap on tax increases for commercial properties and second homes. Florida's lack of state income tax means municipalities depend heavily on property tax revenue; the changes are expected to cost local governments $4.6 billion annually by 2027, escalating to nearly $12 billion by 2032.
stories.impact: South Florida and statewide: reduced municipal tax revenue will constrain funding for schools, infrastructure, and services that support population growth and economic development—potentially dampening demand-side rent growth drivers. However, lower property taxes on primary residences may accelerate owner-occupancy and reduce rental supply if existing renters purchase, creating a modest supply-side tailwind for multifamily landlords in the near term.

stories.title: Lincoln Purchases 52K-SF Boerne Medical Offices
stories.excerpt: Lincoln Property Co.⁠ and PGIM acquired The Sobo Medical Building in Boerne. The multi-story, 52,000-square-foot medical office on Herff Road is 93% leased to a mix of healthcare providers and specialists. The medical center is operated by Baptist Health System and the Surgery Center of Boerne. Baptist Brain & Spine Neurosurgery is also among the entities housed in the Sobo. The San Antonio Business Journal reports that Perardi Development had confirmed plans for a multi-story medical campus along Herff Road near South Main Street in Boerne. That project is expected to include a mix of healthcare, wellness and retail space. The three-story tower, branded Wellness Plaza, will span 37,000 square feet and cost roughly $14 million to construct. Perardi has an option on another 8 acres next to the planned Wellness Plaza site and is already contemplating an expansion to include a second tower roughly double the size of the first. bullets: Lincoln Property/PGIM acquire 52K-SF Sobo Medical Building in Boerne, Texas; 93% leased
Baptist Health System operates center; Perardi Development plans adjacent $14M Wellness Plaza (37K SF)

stories.summary: Lincoln Property Company and PGIM acquired The Sobo Medical Building, a 52,000-square-foot medical office in Boerne, Texas, currently 93% leased to healthcare providers including Baptist Brain & Spine Neurosurgery and Surgery Center of Boerne. Adjacent developer Perardi Development is planning a $14 million, 37,000-square-foot Wellness Plaza and holds an option on 8 acres for a potential second tower roughly double the size, signaling strong healthcare real estate demand in the Boerne submarket.
stories.impact: San Antonio/Boerne: clustering of healthcare, wellness, and medical office development on Herff Road indicates sustained job and population growth supporting professional services demand. Multifamily developers should monitor in-migration of healthcare workers and families relocating for employment at these expanding medical facilities and the broader San Antonio market's job diversification away from military-dependent economy.

stories.title: Core, Midloch Acquire Celebrated Denver Shopping Center
stories.excerpt: Core Acquisitions and Midloch Investment Partners⁠ purchased the 271,632-square-foot Lamar Station Plaza property on Wednesday for $30.25 million. The shopping center, at 6431-6791 W. Colfax Ave., was 76% occupied at the time of the sale. Broadstreet was the seller. The Denver Business Journal reports that the center is home to Casa Bonita, a famed eatery that attracts more than 650,000 visits a year. The 1,100-seat restaurant features live entertainment, such as cliff divers and an indoor waterfall. Other tenants at the center include Planet Fitness⁠, Ross Dress for Less⁠, Dollar Tree, Dutch Bros coffee and Arc Thrift Stores, alongside other local restaurant, service and specialty tenants. Core plans to make improvements such as roof replacements and upgrades to the facade. Cushman & Wakefield the sale to Core Acquisitions and Midloch Investment. The buyers secured a new mortgage loan from Old National Bank. The property will be managed by an affiliate of Core. Cushman & Wakefield will handle leasing for the landlord, the companies said. The post Core, Midloch Acquire Celebrated Denver Shopping Center appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Core Acquisitions/Midloch acquire 271K-SF Lamar Station Plaza, Denver, for $30.25M at 76% occupancy

stories.summary: Core Acquisitions and Midloch Investment Partners purchased Lamar Station Plaza, a 271,632-square-foot shopping center in Denver, for $30.25 million at 76% occupancy. The center's anchor tenant, Casa Bonita, draws over 650,000 visits annually and features live entertainment; other tenants include Planet Fitness, Ross Dress for Less, Dollar Tree, and Dutch Bros. Buyers plan capital improvements including roof and facade upgrades and have secured financing from Old National Bank.
stories.impact: Denver: while primarily a retail play, the acquisition signals confidence in West Colfax Avenue's mixed-use node and stable foot traffic from entertainment/dining anchors, which can support adjacent multifamily density if retail-to-residential conversion or ground-floor retail in new apartments becomes feasible. No direct demand signal, but stable retail fundamentals reduce vacancy risk in mixed-use developments in this submarket.

stories.title: Affinius Lends $226M on Newly Completed Brooklyn Rental Tower
stories.excerpt: Affinius Capital LLC has originated a $226-million loan to refinance 55 Willoughby (marketed as House 55), a Class A, 295-unit, 43-story multifamily property with 3,200 square feet of ground-floor retail located in Downtown Brooklyn. The loan was made to a joint venture between Lonicera Partners and Rabina. Proceeds will bridge the property to stabilization early next year. “55 Willoughby offers what we look for in an investment: a high-quality asset in a supply-constrained submarket, backed by sponsors with a proven record,” said Affinius executive director Perry Katz. “This financing gives Lonicera and Rabina the flexibility to complete lease-up and execute their business plan as the property moves toward stabilization.” Located at 55 Willoughby St. on the border of Downtown Brooklyn and Brooklyn Heights, the property offers immediate access to the Jay Street–MetroTech transit hub, major employment hubs, and entertainment, while providing a relatively affordable alternative to Midtown Manhattan. stories.summary: Affinius Capital originated a $226 million refinance loan on House 55 (55 Willoughby), a newly completed 295-unit Class A multifamily tower in Downtown Brooklyn with 3,200 square feet of ground-floor retail. The 43-story property, developed by a joint venture of Lonicera Partners and Rabina, is located at the border of Downtown Brooklyn and Brooklyn Heights near the Jay Street–MetroTech transit hub and major employment centers, marketed as a relatively affordable alternative to Midtown Manhattan. Proceeds will bridge the property to lease-up stabilization in early 2025.
stories.impact: Downtown Brooklyn: strong capital availability for stabilizing Class A multifamily assets signals continued investor appetite for transit-proximate, supply-constrained Brooklyn submarkets. The property's positioning as a more affordable Manhattan alternative reinforces demand for rental housing from Manhattan-displaced professionals, supporting rent growth and occupancy in the Downtown Brooklyn/Brooklyn Heights corridor.

stories.title: Chinese Language Preschool to Open Second NYC Site in FiDi
stories.excerpt: Ya Ya Mandarin Immersion Preschool, which offers all-Mandarin educational programs for young children, will open its second Manhattan preschool in the Financial District. The preschool has signed a 10-year lease for 4,640 square feet at 9-15 Dutch Street, a six-story commercial and residential building owned by Time Equities, according to broker RTL. Ya Ya will likely replace preschool Downtown Little School, which closed in the space in 2024. The deal, which had an asking rent of $50 per square foot, represents Ya Ya’s second spot in Manhattan, following its first location at 291 Broadway in Tribeca. The preschool was founded in 2008 with the goal to teach toddlers Mandarin through music and activities. RTL’s Thomas Galo, who represented the tenant alongside Matthew Knispel, said the Financial District is “a wonderful place” for the preschool’s new location. “More families are choosing to call Lower Manhattan home, and they’re looking for exceptional schools close by,” Galo said in a statement. “Ya Ya offers something truly special, and it will be a fantastic addition to the community.” A spokesperson for Ya Ya added that the new Dutch Street spot allows it to “bring its programs to more Downtown families.” There were no landlord brokers in this deal. A spokesperson for Time Equities did not immediately respond to a request for comment. It’s also unclear when the preschool will move into its new location between Fulton and John streets, but it will join an array of retail tenants on the block, including 7th Street Burger, Apollo Bagels and gym F45 Training. Isabelle Durso can be reached at idurso@commercialobserver.com.

stories.summary: Ya Ya Mandarin Immersion Preschool signed a 10-year lease for 4,640 square feet at 9-15 Dutch Street in the Financial District at $50 per square foot, marking its second Manhattan location after opening in Tribeca. Ya Ya replaces Downtown Little School, which closed in 2024. RTL brokers noted that more families are choosing Lower Manhattan as home and seeking exceptional schools nearby, indicating a shift in residential preferences for the neighborhood.
stories.impact: Lower Manhattan/Financial District: family-oriented tenant expansions (preschool, retail amenities) are trailing indicators of residential population growth and demographic shift toward younger families. This signals underlying multifamily demand strength in FiDi and validates new residential development pipelines; developers should monitor family-serving retail tenants as demand markers for mixed-use and residential ground-floor programming.

stories.title: Northmarq Arranges $17M Sale, $14M Acquisition Financing for Omaha MF
stories.excerpt: Northmarq’s Midwest Multifamily Investment Sales team of Parker Stewart, Anthony Martinez, Dominic Martinez and Alex Malzone, with Jim Gibson, brokered the $9.4 million sale of Southfield Apartments. The 84-unit multifamily complex was built in 1993 and is located at 7009 S 83rd St. in La Vista, Nebraska. Northmarq represented the seller, an Omaha-based private investor in the transaction. The buyer was a Dallas-based private investor. Northmarq’s Debt + Equity team, led by John Reed, secured the financing through its in-house Fannie Mae DUS platform. The transaction was structured on a 5-year term. Southfield Apartments features a mix of one-, two- and three-bedroom apartments in the growing community of La Vista, just 15 minutes south of downtown Omaha. Proximate to Interstate 80, the property provides convenient access to Omaha’s top employers, major retailers, entertainment options and other key economic drivers in the area. A Dallas-based private investor acquired the property from an Omaha-based owner. Northmarq's Debt + Equity team secured $14 million in acquisition financing through its Fannie Mae DUS platform on a 5-year term. The property offers convenient access to I-80 and Omaha's top employers.
stories.impact: Omaha metro/La Vista: continued investor appetite for secondary-market workforce housing near I-80 corridor and major employment centers, even for older (1993-built) assets, suggests sustained demand from in-migration and stable employment fundamentals. Out-of-state buyer (Dallas) signals Omaha's appeal as a value play; developers should monitor supply pipeline and absorption in suburban corridors like La Vista as the market tightens.

stories.title: Boutique Arlington Heights Apartments Sell for $25M
stories.excerpt: JLL has arranged the $25 million sale of FourNorth Apartments, a 76-unit boutique apartment community in Arlington Heights, Illinois. JLL worked exclusively on behalf of the seller, Benchmark Developers, in the sale of the property to a private investor. JLL’s Capital Markets Investment Sales and Advisory team representing the seller was led by Bill Baumann, David Gaines and Sam Grohe. Completed in 2024, FourNorth Apartments offers studio, one- and two-bedroom units averaging 796 square feet. The five-story, pet-friendly building is 95% occupied. FourNorth Apartments is located at 4 North Hickory Road within walking distance of the shops, restaurants and entertainment options in Downtown Arlington Heights. “FourNorth Apartments attracted a significant amount of investor interest due to the core quality of the asset itself, as well as its unbeatable suburban location in Arlington Heights, an affluent northwest suburb of Chicago that also boasts fantastic market fundamentals with just one other property built within the last five years,” said Baumann. stories.summary: JLL's Capital Markets Investment Sales team arranged the $25 million sale of FourNorth Apartments, a newly completed 76-unit boutique apartment community in Arlington Heights, Illinois, on behalf of seller Benchmark Developers. The five-story, pet-friendly building is 95% occupied and features studio, one-, and two-bedroom units averaging 796 square feet. Located at 4 North Hickory Road within walking distance of Downtown Arlington Heights retail and dining, the property sold to a private investor.

The scarcity of recent competitive inventory (only one other property built in past five years) supports rent growth; developers should prioritize well-located Arlington Heights submarkets for new construction.

stories.title: Berkadia Provides $219M to Rehab Rangel Houses in New York City
stories.excerpt: Genesis Companies has secured $669 million in financing to rehabilitate Rangel Houses, a 984-unit public housing complex in New York City, Commercial Observer can first report. Berkadia provided $219 million in first-mortgage debt that is backed by Fannie Mae, while the New York City Housing Authority (NYCHA) and the New York City Housing Development Corporation (HDC) provided $214 million in development financing, with an additional $94.5 million provided through federal and state tax credit equity. Goldman Sachs provided an undisclosed tax credit investment. Berkadia’s Matthew Baptiste and Heather Olson arranged the financing. Berkadia’s Fannie Mae loan features a 15-year term, including five years of interest-only payments, and is expected to blend Rental Assistance Demonstration (RAD) debt with Section 18 programs to rehabilitate the affordable housing complex. All units in the building hold residents earning at or below 80 percent of the area median income. Baptiste described the financing in a statement as “a highly coordinated capital structure that combines public subsidies, tax credit equity and agency financing.” Located at 159-16 Harlem River Drive in Upper Manhattan, Rangel Houses opened in 1951 as an 11-acre public housing campus. The complex is structured as eight high-rise elevator buildings that serve as home to more than 1,800 residents. Karim Hutson, president and CEO of Genesis Companies, said that his firm plans “comprehensive renovations” to update and modernize nearly 1,000 apartment units and improve a complex that includes playgrounds, commercial space, a senior center, a day care center, and a youth center. “This closing represents years of work to bring together the resources and partners needed to make a transformative investment in Rangel Houses,” added Hutson. Brian Pascus can be reached at bpascus@commercialobserver.com.

stories.summary: Genesis Companies secured $669 million in financing to rehabilitate Rangel Houses, a 984-unit public housing complex in New York City. Berkadia provided $219 million in Fannie Mae-backed first-mortgage debt (15-year term, 5 years interest-only), while NYCHA and New York City Housing Development Corporation provided $214 million in development financing and $94.5 million in federal and state tax credit equity (with Goldman Sachs as tax credit investor). The financing structure blends Rental Assistance Demonstration (RAD) and Section 18 programs to preserve affordability for residents earning at or below 80% of area median income.
stories.impact: New York City: large-scale public housing preservation financing underscores continued capital availability for affordable multifamily under federal subsidy programs and tax credit structures. While not directly competitive with market-rate development, the scale and structure (public-private capital stacking) reflect strong institutional appetite for New York housing and signal lower-risk, lower-return asset class momentum—context for market-rate developers competing for land and labor.

stories.title: Grow Therapy Signs 78K-SF Office Lease at Essex Crossing
stories.excerpt: An office lease representing expanded access to mental health care caught the attention of Gov. Kathy Hochul on Wednesday. Grow Therapy, a mental health platform offering in-person and online therapy, has signed another New York City office lease — its second in only a year — for more than 78,000 square feet at 145 Delancey Street within Essex Crossing, according to an announcement from the governor’s office. Grow Therapy plans to invest $15 million in the space and create 123 new jobs. The landlords — a joint venture involving Taconic Partners, L+M Development Partners, BFC Partners, the Prusik Group and Goldman Sachs Urban Investment Group — did not immediately provide the asking rent, the length of the lease or the names of brokers in the deal. The average office asking rent for Lower Manhattan was $62.40 per square foot in the third quarter of 2026, according to a report from CBRE. “Grow Therapy’s decision to deepen its roots here reflects the strength of our talent and innovation economy, and we are proud to support a company using technology to expand access to mental health care while creating new opportunities for New Yorkers,” Hochul said in a statement. In early November 2025, Grow Therapy signed a lease for 19,000 square feet at Northwood Investors’ 100 Broadway, which gave the telehealth service the space to hire 186 new employees focusing mainly on technology, operations and marketing. “When I joined Grow this year, the momentum was already underway,” Grow Therapy Chief Financial Officer Seth Bressack said in a statement. “Sustaining it is our top priority, and New York is our center of gravity: What we build in this city reaches everyone we serve in all 50 states. The talent is here, the clients are here, and now more of the jobs will be too.” The firm is expanding with the $1.4 million backing of the Empire State Development’s Excelsior Jobs Program tax credits. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.

stories.summary: Grow Therapy, a mental health platform providing in-person and online therapy services, signed a second New York City office lease in one year for more than 78,000 square feet at 145 Delancey Street within Essex Crossing (Lower Manhattan). Grow Therapy plans to invest $15 million in the space and create 123 new jobs. The landlord joint venture includes Taconic Partners, L+M Development Partners, BFC Partners, the Prusik Group, and Goldman Sachs Urban Investment Group. Governor Kathy Hochul highlighted the announcement as supporting mental health care access expansion.
stories.impact: Lower Manhattan/Financial District: rapid office lease expansion (two leases in 12 months) by a high-growth, mission-driven tech/services company signals sustained demand for downtown office space and talent concentration. While office-focused, this suggests underlying workforce population and amenity investments (healthcare services) that support adjacent multifamily demand; developers should track health-tech and services-sector employment clustering as demand markers for residential in mixed-use Lower Manhattan projects.
